meta.headline: **Partial implementation (B)** is the dominant outcome (145 of 234 recommendations), and Tajikistan gives a detailed National Report: the Equality and Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Act (2022, **A**), the National Human Rights Strategy to 2038 (2023, **A**), a National Programme on the Protection of Children's Rights 2026-2030 (**A**), a complete ban on corporal punishment (2024), a new disability-rights Act (June 2026), a 92% budget increase for the Commissioner for Human Rights, amendments to the Domestic Violence Act and a State Programme 2025-2030, trafficking and child-labour plans, and amendments to the Criminal Code on online expression (May 2025). **No relevant action (C)** persists on criminalising domestic violence (still in the draft Criminal Code), the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and other ratifications, torture investigations, religious freedom, LGBTI protection and a standing invitation to special procedures. **Contrary measures (E)** apply to 16 recommendations on civil society, media and political prisoners: the UN reports 700 NGOs liquidated in 18 months, about 20 journalists and bloggers imprisoned since 2022 and websites blocked.

recommendations.text: Continue the national efforts to prevent juvenile delinquency or juveniles from joining terrorist and extremist movements

Operationalize the recently drawn-up human rights and development plans

Continue efforts to implement the National Development Strategy for the period up to 2030

themes.theme: Human rights education, trainings & awareness raising

blocks.summary: Human rights awareness-raising and training
blocks.rationale: 2024 was declared the Year of Legal Literacy and a legal literacy course was introduced in higher education.

recommendations.text: Maintain its awareness-raising and training activities on human rights for the general public to raise legal awareness across the country

Continue systematic work to further strengthen the judicial and legal system
Implement the 11 recommendations from the previous cycle on the right to a fair trial, the independence of the judiciary and measures to protect lawyers

recommendations.text: Revise the Law on the Commissioner for Human Rights and bring the institution into full compliance with the Paris Principles
Further strengthen the independence of the national human rights mechanism in line with Paris Principles
Consider strengthening the national human rights institution, the Commissioner for Human Rights, in accordance with the Paris Principles
Strengthen efforts to achieve the compliance of the Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman) with the Paris Principles

recommendations.text: Consider implementing measures to upgrade the Office of the Commissioner for Human Rights to an A status institution in line with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights

blocks.summary: Protect religious minorities, LGBTI persons and people living with HIV from discrimination
blocks.rationale: The 2022 Equality Act does not list sexual orientation or gender identity; the CESCR and civil society report continuing discrimination and police abuse of LGBT+ persons.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 93 — COC Netherlands: "the law did not explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) as protected grounds"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 90 — JS11: "police often arbitrarily detained LGBT+ people"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 93 — Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights: "called upon the Government to provide effective protection against all forms of discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity"

recommendations.text: Cease discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons based on their sexual orientation or gender identity and actively work towards the eradication of societal homophobia and transphobia

Provide effective protection against all forms of discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, both in law and in practice, and conduct awareness-raising campaigns to combat the stigma affecting lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex persons
Take measures to eliminate discrimination and abuse based on people’s sexual orientation and gender identity

blocks.summary: Combat discrimination and violence, including on grounds of gender, disability and HIV status
blocks.rationale: The 2022 Equality Act, the 2024 Domestic Violence Act amendments and the 2026 disability and labour reforms address gender, disability and employment discrimination; sexual orientation and gender identity are not covered.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 34 — Tajikistan: "The Equality and Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Act defines direct and indirect discrimination"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 93 — COC Netherlands: "the law did not explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) as protected grounds"

recommendations.text: Take the necessary steps to combat discrimination and violence against women and children, and on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity
Take concrete measures to combat all forms of discrimination and violence, including domestic violence, based on gender, sexual orientation and gender identity

blocks.summary: Review laws affecting freedom of religion or belief
blocks.rationale: The 2022 amendments to the Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations Act restrict founders and staff; the Special Rapporteur and civil society call for review and report raids on minority churches.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 99 — Tajikistan: "In July 2022, amendments were made to the Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations Act"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 14 — Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief: "review the Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations Act and the Act on Regulating Traditions, Celebrations and Rituals with a view to bringing them into compliance with international standards"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 63 — ECLJ: "Baptist, Evangelical, and Pentecostal churches being raided, threatened, fined, and their members arrested"

recommendations.text: Guarantee freedom of religion or belief and eliminate all forms of discrimination against people belonging to religious minorities

blocks.summary: Adopt comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation
blocks.rationale: The Equality and Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Act was adopted on 19 July 2022, defines direct and indirect discrimination and gives a right to compensation; the Commissioner is the competent body.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 34 — Tajikistan: "The Equality and Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Act defines direct and indirect discrimination"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 22 — United Nations country team: "had adopted the Law on equality and elimination of all forms of discrimination, establishing a comprehensive legal framework prohibiting direct, indirect and multiple discrimination"

recommendations.text: Introduce comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation and legal framework

blocks.summary: Address stigmatisation and discrimination against people living with HIV
blocks.rationale: The Health Code was amended (December 2025) and the Supreme Court issued guidance (December 2023) on HIV transmission cases; mandatory testing and criminal liability remain.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 155 — Tajikistan: "persons living with HIV who are receiving antiretroviral therapy and have achieved an undetectable viral load are considered not to present a risk to their sexual partners"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 64 — Human Rights Center TJ: "Laws such as mandatory testing of people living with HIV allowed discriminatory treatment toward certain groups"

recommendations.text: Take concrete steps to address the stigmatization and discrimination faced by persons living with HIV/AIDS, including in law and in practice

blocks.summary: Prevent and respond to domestic violence
blocks.rationale: The Domestic Violence Act was amended (2024) to broaden the definition of violence, a State Programme 2025-2030 and an Interdepartmental Council (February 2025) were created, support centres expanded and 21 prevention-officer posts introduced; the offence is not yet in the Criminal Code.

recommendations.text: Continue working towards combating gender-based violence by taking measures to criminalize such actions and establishing reporting mechanisms
Develop a comprehensive strategy and action plan to eliminate all forms of gender-based violence against women and adopt laws criminalizing all forms of gender-based violence

blocks.summary: Combat gender-based violence
blocks.rationale: The Domestic Violence Act was amended (2024), a State Programme 2025-2030 adopted and an Interdepartmental Council created (February 2025); the Criminal Code criminalisation remains in draft.

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 31 — Tajikistan: "the Interdepartmental Council on the Prevention of Domestic Violence was established under the Government of Tajikistan"

recommendations.text: Step up efforts to address all forms of gender-based violence, including domestic violence, including by intensifying awareness campaigns and training for duty bearers

themes.theme: Economic, social & cultural rights - general measures of implementation

blocks.summary: Skills and economic participation of youth and women
blocks.rationale: A presidential grants programme for women entrepreneurs and a State Employment Promotion Programme 2023-2027 were launched.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 185 — Tajikistan: "15 million somoni are allocated to fund 200 presidential grants"

recommendations.text: Continue to implement skills development programmes to facilitate the economic participation of youth and women

blocks.summary: Combat corruption
blocks.rationale: The National Report mentions only a Code of Ethics for Judges.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 91 — Tajikistan: "A Code of Ethics for Judges is in force, aimed at preventing the risks of corruption and enhancing public confidence in the justice system"

recommendations.text: Intensify efforts to combat corruption

blocks.summary: Sustainable development and social security
blocks.rationale: Poverty fell from 56% (2010) to under 20% and a Social Protection Development Strategy up to 2040 was approved (2022).
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 41 — Tajikistan: "the poverty rate fell from 56% in 2010 to less than 20% in recent years"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 135 — Tajikistan: "The Social Protection Development Strategy for the period up to 2040 was approved by a government decision of 29 November 2022"

recommendations.text: Continue to promote sustainable economic and social development and to improve people’s living standards, so as to provide a solid foundation for people to enjoy human rights
Continue consolidating actions that promote the right to social security and formal employment

blocks.summary: Participation in climate and disaster risk reduction
blocks.rationale: Women, children and persons with disabilities are involved through the Women and Water Forum, rural-women adaptation grants and a disability needs analysis.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 58 — Tajikistan: "The State actively promotes the participation of women in climate-related decisionmaking"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 60 — Tajikistan: "a situational analysis was conducted of the needs of persons with disabilities during climate-related emergencies"

recommendations.text: Ensure the meaningful participation of women, children, persons with disabilities and local communities in the development and implementation of climate change and disaster risk reduction frameworks

blocks.rationale: The Domestic Violence Act was amended (2024) to broaden the definition of violence, a State Programme 2025-2030 and an Interdepartmental Council (February 2025) were created, support centres expanded and 21 prevention-officer posts introduced; the offence is not yet in the Criminal Code.

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 31 — Tajikistan: "the Interdepartmental Council on the Prevention of Domestic Violence was established under the Government of Tajikistan"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 71 — JS5: "domestic violence has yet to be recognized as a criminal offence in Tajikistan"

recommendations.text: Address domestic violence and guarantee that the perpetrators are brought to court in line with Sustainable Development Goal 3
Sustain efforts to prevent domestic violence, support victims and take legal action against perpetrators of domestic violence

blocks.summary: Investigate and prosecute torture and ill-treatment
blocks.rationale: The UN country team reports that victims do not receive effective remedies and courts have no established practice of excluding evidence obtained by torture; JS10 reports that judges rarely order investigations.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 27 — United Nations country team: "torture and ill-treatment remained persistent and that, in practice, victims did not receive effective remedies or adequate compensation"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 30 — JS10: "Judges rarely ordered thorough investigations into allegations of torture and ill-treatment"

recommendations.text: Ensure that excessive use of force, including ill-treatment and torture, by law enforcement officials at the time of arrest and during interrogations is investigated and prosecuted and perpetrators convicted and held accountable

Ensure that thorough and impartial investigations are carried out into all deaths in custody as well as all allegations of torture and ill-treatment, and implement the recommendations of the Special Rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, based on his country visits

blocks.summary: Protect LGBTI persons in law and practice
blocks.rationale: The 2022 Equality Act does not list sexual orientation or gender identity; the CESCR and civil society report arbitrary detention and ill-treatment of LGBT+ persons and no measure is reported.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 93 — COC Netherlands: "the law did not explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) as protected grounds"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 90 — JS11: "police often arbitrarily detained LGBT+ people"

recommendations.text: Hold accountable officials, public figures and authors of media and online publications calling for violence and hate speech against LGBTI+ persons

blocks.summary: Address persecution of dissent and lawyers
blocks.rationale: The National Report contains no reply; L4L reports harassment and detention of lawyers, and HFHR PCP reports intimidation, surveillance and long sentences on politically motivated charges.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 44 — L4L: "attempts to harass and disrupt the work of lawyers in Tajikistan"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 50 — HFHR PCP: "an ongoing narrowing of civic space marked by growing restrictions on freedom of expression, association and assembly"

recommendations.text: Duly address allegations of systemic persecution against opposition figures, journalists, lawyers and human rights defenders

blocks.summary: Protect civil society and human rights defenders; remove restrictions on associations
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: In November 2023 the Minister of Justice announced that 700 NGOs had been liquidated within 18 months, and rights defenders, journalists and activists have been imprisoned: measures contrary to the recommendations.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 41 — United Nations country team: "700 non-governmental organizations in Tajikistan had been liquidated over an 18-month period"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 41 — Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights defenders: "signalled a deteriorating environment for civil society and human rights defence in Tajikistan"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 53 — HRW: "an end to all politically motivated closures of NGOs and civil society organizations"

recommendations.text: Cease reprisals, violence and pressure on political opposition, civil society activists, human rights non-governmental organizations, journalists and members of their families

blocks.summary: Release imprisoned journalists and activists; stop harassment of journalists
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: Around 20 independent journalists and bloggers have been imprisoned since 2022, often on terrorism or extremism charges, and HRW and JS14 call for the release of those imprisoned over the GBAO protests.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/2), para. 43 — United Nations country team: "around 20 independent journalists and bloggers had been imprisoned, often on terrorism- or extremism-related charges"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 58 — HRW: "immediately and unconditionally release all HRDs, lawyers, journalists, and civil society activists imprisoned"

recommendations.text: Stop harassment of journalists and ensure the protection of the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion

blocks.summary: Guarantee the independence and safety of lawyers
blocks.rationale: The Bar and Advocacy Act was amended in January 2024 to strengthen the legal status and independence of lawyers; L4L reports continuing harassment.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 92 — Tajikistan: "amendments were made to the Bar and Advocacy Act to strengthen the legal status and independence of lawyers"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 45 — L4L: "ensure that sufficient safeguards are in place, both in law and in practice, to guarantee the full independence and safety of lawyers"

recommendations.text: Ensure that lawyers are guaranteed full independence and safety, in law and in practice, to carry out their legitimate duties without any harassment, undue interference or fear of arbitrary criminal prosecution or other retaliatory measures

blocks.summary: Improve prison conditions and allow independent monitoring
blocks.rationale: The Commissioner's monitoring group was enlarged to 30 members including civil society, and a Penal Correction System Reform Strategy to 2030 is being implemented; JS1 calls for access for all independent monitors.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 85 — Tajikistan: "Since 2025, the group’s membership has been increased to 30 people to include representatives from civil society"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 82 — Tajikistan: "The Penal Correction System Reform Strategy in the period up to 2030 is being implemented"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 34 — JS1: "advised the government to allow independent monitoring of all detention facilities"

recommendations.by: the Nelson Mandela Rules; United States of America
recommendations.text: Permit more access to independent prison monitoring organizations including private and fully confidential interviews with prisoners, consistent with the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners

Improve conditions in prisons in line with the Nelson Mandela Rules and provide access to the International Committee of the Red Cross. Investigate all cases of prison riots, allegations of torture and ill-treatment and deaths in custody
Implement the United Nations Rules for the Treatment of Women Prisoners and Non-custodial Measures for Women Offenders (the Bangkok Rules) in order to address the special needs of women in prisons

blocks.summary: Dialogue with civil society on prison reform
blocks.rationale: Civil society representatives joined the Commissioner's monitoring group (2025) and the NGO list for prison visits was expanded in 2022.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 85 — Tajikistan: "Since 2025, the group’s membership has been increased to 30 people to include representatives from civil society"

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 108 — Tajikistan: "the list of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) participating in the Monitoring Group of the Office of the Human Right Commission for visits to closed institutions was significantly expanded"

recommendations.text: Continue advancing in the dialogue with civil society and non-governmental organizations to deepen the necessary reform of the prison system, as well as to extend these good practices of dialogue with associations to other areas of the fight against torture and cruel treatment

themes.theme: Prohibition of torture & ill-treatment (including cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

blocks.summary: Strengthen the fight against torture
blocks.rationale: Supreme Court Decision No. 32 (December 2025) guides compensation for torture victims and interrogation rooms are being equipped with audiovisual recording; JS10 reports torture remains widespread.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 78 — Tajikistan: "adopted Decision No. 32, which provided courts with clear guidance on the compensation for harm suffered by victims of torture"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 30 — JS10: "torture and ill-treatment remained widespread in Tajikistan, especially in police custody and pre-trial detention"

recommendations.text: Strengthen the fight against torture and ill-treatment
Strengthen measures to prevent episodes of torture and enforced disappearances

recommendations.text: Release all journalists who have been imprisoned on politically motivated charges

Release all political activists, lawyers and journalists arrested for arbitrary reasons, extend the procedural guarantees put in place to the procedures and conditions of police custody, and apply systematically in practice the new legal guarantees relating to notification and registration following an arrest

blocks.summary: Prevent arbitrary detention and release political detainees
blocks.rationale: The National Report restates existing custody safeguards (72-hour limit, lawyer from detention); journalists, lawyers and activists remain imprisoned.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 73 — Tajikistan: "Detention without a court decision is limited to 72 hours for adults and 48 hours for minors"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 33 — JS10: "reduce the period of detention before the remand hearing from the current 72 to 48"

recommendations.text: Develop transparent procedures to prevent and address arbitrary detentions and ensure the right to a fair trial, including unhindered access to legal representation, free from the threat of government interference

blocks.summary: Extend amnesty releases to political prisoners
blocks.rationale: The June 2026 Amnesty Act applies to 18,038 convicted persons, with leniency for women and minors; no release of political prisoners is reported.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/1), para. 88 — Tajikistan: "In June 2026, the President signed the Amnesty Act, which applies to 18,038 convicted persons"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TJK/3), para. 58 — HRW: "immediately and unconditionally release all HRDs, lawyers, journalists, and civil society activists imprisoned"

recommendations.text: Extend the measure of releasing detainees, in the context of the amnesty law, to political prisoners

themes.theme: Freedom of opinion and expression & access to information

blocks.summary: Guarantee freedom of expression and media freedom
blocks.rationale: Tajikistan amended articles 179(3) and 307(1) of the Criminal Code (May 2025) to remove penalties for 'liking' extremist content; stakeholders report a steep deterioration of press freedom and a narrowing of civic space.

Ensure freedom of expression and the freedom of the media, including on the Internet, in accordance with international human rights norms

Guarantee the rights to freedom of expression, assembly and peaceful association, as well as the freedom of the press, first of all by releasing political activists, lawyers and journalists detained on arbitrary grounds

meta.caveat: The Human Rights Committee's follow-up procedure grades only the two to four “priority” recommendations it selected from this country's Concluding Observations (CoBs). The other CoBs are not graded.

paragraphs.title: Surveillance and interception of private communications

limbs.eval: While taking note of the information provided on the current legislative framework on data protection, the Committee regrets the lack of information on action taken to ensure that all legislation is in full conformity with the Covenant. It reiterates its recommendation and requests specific information on action taken to that end since the adoption of the concluding observations. The Committee takes note of the information regarding the designation in 2020 of the Communication Service of the Government of as the competent body for personal data protection and the requirement for a certificate of compliance to collect and process personal data. Nevertheless, it regrets that all information and communications continue to flow through the single communications switching centre controlled by the government Communication Service and that no action has been taken to ensure that surveillance and interception is conducted subject to judicial authorization and to effective and independent oversight. It reiterates its recommendation. The Committee takes note of the information concerning article 42 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the compensation provided for material damage found to have been caused. Nevertheless, it regrets the lack of information on specific steps taken since the adoption of the concluding observations to ensure that the persons affected have proper access to effective remedies in cases of abuse. It reiterates its recommendations and requests statistical information on the number of cases of abuse and the remedies applied

limbs.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
limbs.eval: The Committee regrets the absence of information on steps taken towards the decriminalization of insulting or libelling the President/leader of the nation and insulting other State officials. It also regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, individuals have been deprived of their liberty on a number of such charges, including for insulting State officials. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. While taking note of the information on the existing legislation providing State guarantees of media freedom and independence, the Committee regrets that independent media reportedly continue to be scarce and that media outlets have been blocked or forced to cease covering the protests in Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region after receiving threats of closure from the Prosecutor General’s Office. It also regrets that State-owned media are reportedly increasingly engaging in State propaganda. It therefore reiterates its recommendation. The Committee takes note of the State party’s statement that the laws in force are entirely consistent with its international obligations. Nevertheless, the Committee regrets that no steps have been taken during the reporting period to repeal or amend the laws and regulations providing for the restrictions referred to by the Committee in its concluding observations, with a view to bringing them into full compliance with the Covenant, and that the State party has shown no intention of doing so. It reiterates its recommendation. While taking note of the measures in place to provide access to information, the Committee regrets that it has reportedly become more challenging for journalists to receive information from State bodies, frequently having to wait two to three months to receive a response to their information requests to the authorities, and that 37 out of 58 written information requests submitted in July and August 2021 remain unanswered. It is particularly concerned at reports of the continuous Internet shutdowns and blocking of websites between August 2021 and April 2022, including the short-term blocking of the Asia Plus and Radio Ozodi news outlets and of Facebook, and at the reports that the Internet and mobile phone network were shut down in the Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region until the end of June 2022 following the violent dispersal of protestors in Khorog in May 2022, which left one person dead and several wounded. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. The Committee regrets the absence of information on action taken by the State party to ensure that journalists and media workers are effectively protected against intimidation. Furthermore, it particularly regrets that a number of independent journalists and bloggers were reportedly arrested on extremism or terrorism charges and accused of having ties with the banned opposition parties following the protests in Gorno-Badakhshan autonomous region in May 2022. It also particularly regrets that no one has reportedly been held accountable for the violent attack against four journalists by unidentified men in plain clothes in May 2022 after they interviewed another journalist and all of their equipment containing the recorded interviews was confiscated. The Committee reiterates its recommendation and requests information on specific measures taken to investigate and prosecute those responsible for any intimidation of or threats or violence against independent journalists and media workers, including the above-mentioned attack in May 2022

The Committee takes note of the information that the media are subject to restrictions only for the purposes of maintaining public order or national security, protecting the rights and freedoms of others or preserving the honour, dignity and reputation of individuals. Nevertheless, it regrets the lack of information provided on steps taken by the State party to lift undue restrictions on the exercise of freedom of expression. It also regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, freedom of expression continues to be severely restricted, both online and offline, and reiterates its recommendation. While taking note of the information that, under article 30 of the Constitution, everyone is entitled to freedom of speech, freedom of the press and the right to use the media, the Committee regrets the lack of information on measures taken to ensure the independence of the broadcasting and licensing authority. It also regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, the authorities continue to put pressure on foreign media outlets by refusing, withdrawing or restricting journalists’ accreditations. It further regrets that, while under article 14 of the Television and Radio Broadcasting Act, both State and independent broadcasters are required to have a licence in order to broadcast, in practice, only private, non-State-owned media outlets are reportedly required to obtain one. It reiterates its recommendation

limbs.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
limbs.eval: While taking note of the information provided that, under the Constitution and election laws, citizens are fully entitled to take part in political life and State governance, the Committee regrets that the elections in March 2020 reportedly took place in a tightly controlled environment, leaving no space for pluralistic political debate and that no genuine political opposition was represented. Furthermore, it regrets that opposition parties and movements reportedly continue to be labelled as extremist and terrorist organizations and were banned from participation in the March 2020 elections. The Committee reiterates its recommendation. The Committee regrets the absence of information provided by the State party with regard to the harassment and exclusion of opposition members from meaningful participation in public life and electoral processes, as well as the investigation into the alleged enforced disappearance of Ehson Odinaev. It also regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, persecution and imprisonment of human rights defenders, opponents of the Government and members of their families for supporting banned opposition parties are ongoing. The Committee reiterates its recommendation and requests specific information on the progress of the investigation into the alleged enforced disappearance of Ehson Odinaev and any results or convictions of those responsible

While taking note of the information received on the election laws in force and the State party’s statement that they are compatible with the Covenant, the Committee regrets the lack of information on the specific steps taken since the adoption of the concluding observations to revise the limitations on the right to stand for election. It also regrets that the restrictive requirements for participation in elections, including those related to residence, language and education, have reportedly not been revised. It reiterates its recommendation. While taking note of the information provided that some convicted persons are not deprived of the right to vote, the Committee regrets that no action has been taken to revise legislation that provides for a blanket denial of the right to vote for all convicted prisoners and any person declared incompetent by a court. It reiterates its recommendation. While taking note of the information regarding the activities and information-sharing of the Central Commission for Elections and Referendums relating to its work, the Committee regrets the absence of information provided by the State party on efforts made to ensure the full independence of the Commission. It also regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, the Commission has not achieved transparency, given that information on important decisions, disaggregated data on voter and candidate registration and data on the distribution of ballots and detailed voting results were not published. Furthermore, the Committee regrets that members of the Commission were reportedly nominated by the President and approved by the parliament without a debate, and that the nomination process lacked transparency, particularly in that the nomination criteria were not public. It reiterates its recommendation. While welcoming the information provided regarding the access to free public broadcasting for political parties and candidates and the corresponding airtime made available to the various political parties, the Committee is concerned that no evidence has reportedly been provided by relevant State bodies or independent observers that the electoral contestants made use of the airtime or print media space guaranteed under the election laws. It regrets that, according to information received by the Committee, in Dushanbe the posters of the President’s Peoples Democratic Party of visible to the public outnumbered the posters of other parties participating in the election. The Committee reiterates its recommendation
